d.title: Six knobs, and what each one is really a decision about
d.caption: **`service_account` is the one to get right first:** everything the deployed agent's tools touch is authorised as that principal, so it wants the narrowest set of roles that works and never the default compute account. **The `env_vars` row carries the mechanism that matters** — a `SecretRef` is resolved at runtime, where a plain string is stored in the engine's spec for anyone with console access to read. And `min_instances=0` is cheap and right for an internal tool; a user-facing agent taking eight seconds to answer its first question of the morning is not.

d.title: The full event stream crosses the boundary, as snake_case dicts
d.caption: **The tool call and the tool result come across, not only the answer**, which is what makes a real interface possible: you can show “checking the weather…” while the tool runs and you have the audit trail client-side. **The cost is that locally you write `event.content.parts[0].function_call.name` and remotely `ev["content"]["parts"][0]["function_call"]["name"]`.** Write one small adapter and keep it in one file — the alternative is dictionary indexing spread through the application, breaking silently on a part kind you did not expect.

d.title: Server-side capability means outside your control
d.caption: **Grounded search returns grounding metadata naming the sources behind each span**, which is what citations and groundedness evaluation are built on, and built-in code execution runs in the provider's sandbox rather than yours. **What you give up is the part to weigh:** no `before_tool_callback` fires, the query is not an argument you can audit in your trace, and the capability does not exist on another provider. A fair trade for provenance and zero integration work; a poor one if you need the queries logged or the agent portable.

d.title: Seven properties, and why each multiplies for an agent
d.caption: **Latency and cost both multiply in ways a single-call benchmark does not show:** a tool-using turn is three round trips, and a conversation resends its history every turn. **And the conclusion is that different agents want different models.** A classifier with `include_contents="none"` and a three-field schema wants the fastest model that gets the enum right; a coordinator deciding between six specialists wants the best routing. They are separate `LlmAgent` objects, so they can be separate models — usually the largest cost saving available.

d.title: Five habits that make a model change a configuration change
d.caption: **Tool descriptions are the part most sensitive to a model change**, because they are prompt — expect to re-tune them, and have the evaluation set that tells you when you are done. **And `FallbackModel` is not a portability plan:** falling back to another provider on failure is a good availability mechanism, but an agent whose tools are tuned for one model may route badly on another, and discovering that during an outage is the worst possible time. Evaluate the fallback path as its own configuration.

d.title: Eight layers, each assuming the one above it failed
d.caption: **That is the whole design principle.** The instruction will be argued with, so the callback checks. The callback may have a bug, so the tool validates. The tool's query may be wrong, so the database filters. **Each layer is cheap and none is sufficient**, and the system is judged by what happens when the model does the worst thing available to it — which is exactly the situation a successful prompt injection creates. Read the right-hand labels as the failure each layer exists to survive.
